Organocatalytic enantio- and diastereoselective
synthesis of trifluoro-ethylamine allenoate
derivatives containing axial and central chiralities†
Siyu Shi, a Mengyun Gu, a Danna Chen, d Ruya Li, b Zhiqiang Shen, ac Jinqi Huang* d
and Wenjin Yan
 *a
Herein, we report an example of a stereoselective c-addition reac-
tion of trifluoromethyl ketimines to 1-alkynyl ketones mediated
by an isothiourea, BTM, under mild conditions, which aﬀorded
tetrasubstituted allenes with central chiralities in high yields (up
to 94% yield), good enantioselectivities (up to 91% ee), and excellent
diastereoselectivities (all420 : 1 dr). In addition, the BTM-catalyzed
c-addition reaction was successfully applied to the gram-scale reac-
tion, and an unexpected benzopyrrolothiazine derivative was success-
fully converted, albeit racemic.
Axial chiral skeletons are widely found in natural products and
drug molecules and are often used as chiral ligands or catalysts
in asymmetric catalysis.
1 Axial chirality refers to the stereo-
isomerization phenomenon (IUPAC) formed by the pairwise
non-coplanar arrangement of four groups around a chiral axis,
and it can be divided into several categories, such as atrop-
isomerism, chiral allenes, and spirocyclic compounds.
2 Among
them, chiral allenes are a special class of molecules with
unique reactivity patterns and have found a certain presence
in natural products and synthetic bioactive molecules such as
medicines (Fig. 1).
1,2 For example, enprostil, which is used to
treat duodenal ulcers, is more than 600 times more active than
its structural analog ( A),
3 and its analog, fenprostalene ( B), is a
commonly used vasodilator used primarily to improve circula-
tion and relieve pain.
4 Acalycixeniolides E (C), a natural product
containing an allene structure extracted from Acalycigorgia
species of coral, has antitumor activity. 5 Zemlicka develops
nucleoside analogs of adenallene ( D), a prototype for cytotoxic
and antiviral drugs currently in the spotlight. 6 Grasshopper
ketone 1 ( E), isolated from the defense secretions of the large
flightless locust Romalea microtera , and citroside A, a natural
product extracted from Cirsium setosum ( F), both have anti-
inflammatory activity. 7,8 The chiral allene units in the above-
mentioned reactive molecules are the key structures where
biological activity is observed.
9
1-Alkynyl ketimines are important synthetics containing
multiple active sites ( a, b, and g).10 In particular, they have
been widely used in synthesizing optically active alkyne-based
a-amino acid derivatives by catalytic asymmetric a-addition
(Scheme 1a).
11 In contrast, selective g-addition of such sub-
strates has been reported less frequently, but the addition
product, alkenylamine, has attracted much attention because
of its potent antiretroviral activity and wide range of applica-
tions. For example, the first example was reported by Wang’s
group et al., which developed a chiral phosphate-catalyzed
g-addition of 2,3-disubstituted indoles to 1-alkynyl ketimines
(Scheme 1b).
12a Lin’s group investigated naphthol’s g-addition
and de-aromatization reactions with 1-alkynyl ketimines. 12b Li’s
group developed isoxazol-5(4 H)-ones with 1-alkynyl ketimines
reactions via chiral phosphoric acid catalysis. 12c More recently,
Zhang’s group asymmetrically synthesized chiral tetrasubstituted

a-aminoenoates with lateral all-ca rbon quaternary stereocenters
via double copper catalysis.12d Ni’s group recently achieved the
pyrrolo[2,1-a] isoquinoline C1-site asymmetric allene functionali-
zation reaction by chiral phosphoric acid. 12e The reported work
involves chiral phosphoric acid and Cu-BOX ligand catalytic
systems, and no chiral Lewis base has been found to mediate
1-alkynyl ketimineg-addition to realize the construction of allenes.
However, isothiourea BTM catalysts,
13 as an essential class of
catalysts in the field of asymmetric organocatalysis in recent years,
are widely used due to their powerful catalytic ability, and the
related work has proliferated.
14
Meanwhile, fluoroalkyl groups are widely used as an important
functional group in pharmaceuticals, pesticides, and functional
materials.
15 They can regulate the metabolic stability, esterophili-
city, and bioavailability of drug molecules. Studies have shown that
adding trifluoromethyl to bioac tive molecules improves mem-
brane permeability.
16 Therefore, the doping of trifluoromethyl
has attracted wide attention, and the technology of trifluoromethyl
synthesis has significantly been developed in recent years.
17
Inspired by these precedents and recent advances in allene
synthesis research, 18 as well as the interest in asymmetric
organocatalytic construction of fluorine-containing compo-
unds,
19 we herein envision a concept of asymmetric g-addition
of trifluoromethyl ketimine to 1-alkynyl ketimine mediated by
isothiourea BTM catalysts to synthesize axial chiral tetrasubsti-
tuted allenes bearing trifluoromethyl groups with controlled
regioselectivity and stereoselectivity, and the methodology suc-
ceeds in remedying the dilemma of having a single catalyst in
the area of allene construction and providing a strong rationale for
the asymmetric construction of allene compounds containing both
c e n t r a la n da x i a lc h i r a l i t y .
To verify the feasibility of our hypothesis, 1-alkynyl ketimine
(1a) and trifluoromethyl ketimine ( 2a) were chosen as the
model substrates. First, various organocatalysts were evaluated,
and the reaction progressed well but with poor enantioselec-
tivity (moderate ee or racemic; see ESI † Table S1). Fortunately,
the reaction could also proceed smoothly when switching to the
isothiourea catalyst C1 (10 mol%), giving the g-addition pro-
duct 3aa not only in 75% yield, but also with an intrinsically
improved enantioselectivity, ee of 83% and dr 420 : 1 (Table 1,
entry 1). Importantly, these results confirmed that the BTM
catalyst could be eﬀective in this transformation. To improve
the yield and enantioselectivity, we first screened the BTM
(Table 1). As expected, both yield and enantioselectivity were
improved when the catalyst structure was appropriately
adjusted (entries 2–8, Table 1), and finally, C5 was determined
to be the most suitable catalyst, which resulted in the g-adduct
3aa in 80% yield, 90% ee and 420 : 1 dr (entry 5, Table 1) in
30 minutes. It is noteworthy that further adjustment of the
solvent significantly increased the yield (to 87%) while the ee
value was unaffected (to 90% ee), and finally, changing the
temperature and adding molecular sieves did not improve the
reaction results (see ESI, † Table S2). Therefore, the optimal
reaction resulted in the g-addition product 3aa in 87% yield
and 90% ee with 2-MeTHF as a solvent for 25 min at room
temperature mediated by catalyst C5.
Subsequently, the scope of the substrates was investigated
under the optimized conditions established. As listed in
Scheme 2, the 1-alkynyl ketimines protected by diﬀerent alkyl
groups reacted smoothly with 2a to aﬀord the products 3ba and
3ca in good yields (80–81%), perfect diastereoselectivities
(420 : 1 dr) and slightly reduced stereoselectivities (87–88%
ee) compared to 3aa. When R was a tert-butyl group, the
reaction system was a mixture, and the target product ( 3da,
Scheme S1, ESI †) was not successfully isolated. Unfortunately,

screening the ester group part observed no better results than
the model reaction. By single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis,
the absolute configuration of3ab was unambiguously established
as the (3 S,5S) stereoisomers, and those of the other allenes were
assigned by analogy.
The following examinations were focused on substituents on
the benzene ring of 1-alkynyl ketimines, and the results are
shown in Scheme 3. Both electron-donating and electron-
withdrawing substituents of 1-alkynyl ketimines worked well
in terms of stereoselectivity (dr values all 420 : 1). The ee values
of the meta-substituents are significantly diminished compared
to the ortho- and para-substituents. For the same substituent
methyl group, its ee is significantly lower in the meta-position
than in the ortho-a n dpara-positions (84vs. 90, 87% ee). However,
there was no significant diﬀerence in the yield (88vs. 87, 88%). Aryl
substrates were tolerated well under standard conditions (85%
yield, 84% ee). Furthermore, the generality of dipole 2 was
evaluated. In general, the enantiomeric excesses of the evalu-
ated substituted ketimines (Scheme 3, 3ab–3ag) were subopti-
mal and lower than those of the modeled reactions (77–88% vs.
90% ee), whereas the yields, reaction times, and diastereoselec-
tivities did not change significantly. In addition to the novel
1.3-dipole above, we studied trifluoromethyl-ketimine derived
from N-Ac isatin ( 2h). Recently, it has been widely used in
asymmetric organocatalysis. Pleasingly, the reaction proceeded
smoothly, and after further optimization of the reaction con-
ditions (see ESI, † Table S2), the g-site addition product 3ah was
obtained in moderate yield (82%) with excellent diastereoselec-
tivity ( 420 : 1 dr) and good excess enantiomeric isomerism
(88% ee). Notably, an evaluation of the ketimine substrate
range revealed that substituents with different electronic pro-
perties (electron-withdrawing or electron-donating groups) and
positions gave g-addition products in moderate to excellent
yields ( 3ah–3ap, 76–94% yield) and perfect dr (all 420 : 1),
however moderate ee values (66–88% ee).
Considering the practicality of this method, we scaled up some
reactions under optimal reaction conditions. As shown in Scheme 4,
the desired products3ea and 3ah were isolated in sacrificial yields
(60 vs. 85%, 70 vs. 82%), respectively, while maintaining enantio-
meric purity (90, 88% ee) and dr values (420 : 1 dr).
Encouraged by the scale-up reactions above, we investigated
the derivatization of 3ea. Fortunately, it was found that un-
expected transformations could be achieved under standard
conditions by simply extending the reaction time without
changing any conditions or further transformations catalyzed
by BTM, as shown in Scheme 4c. The advantage of this syn-
thetic strategy is that the corresponding products can be trans-
formed into valuable benzopyrrolothiazine derivatives 4ea,
whose novel unique frameworks may serve as useful structural
moieties in fragment-based drug discovery. Unfortunately,
this transformation involves unintended racemization of axial
chiral allenes. Given the interesting phenomenon and novelty
of the above derivatization, we next evaluated the general-
izability of the derivatization, as shown in Scheme S3 (see
ESI†), and the single crystal of 4ba showed that the same
reaction
pattern had occurred. The results show that this
transformation has good generalization, excellent diastereos-
electivity, and yields ranging from moderate to high (76–89%).
In addition, several other derivative responses were attempted

but unfortunately failed, as detailed in the supporting informa-
tion document (Scheme S4, see ESI †).
The potential conversion mechanism is shown in Fig. 2: in
the presence of tertiary N atoms of the BTM catalyst, the
trifluoromethyl ketimine undergoes deprotonation and binds
to the catalyst via hydrogen bonding, and then the carbon-
negative ion attacks the highly electrophilic 1-alkynyl ketimines
for g-site-selective addition, resulting in the generation of the
desired axial chiral olefin.
In conclusion, we have demonstrated an asymmetric
g-addition reaction of trifluoromethyl ketimine to 1-alkynyl
ketimines with isothiourea BTM catalysis, which was success-
fully applied to synthesize chiral tetrasubstituted allenes bear-
ing a vicinal central chirality in high yields and with excellent
stereoselectivities (up to 94% yield, 91% ee and 420 : 1 dr)
20
under mild reaction conditions. Moreover, the scale-up of the
reaction and its derivatization proved the synthetic utility of the
scheme, and an unexpected benzopyrrolothiazine derivative
could be converted smoothly, albeit racemic.
